messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas stood in the dim corridor of his second-floor apartment, the heavy deadbolt thrown across the door, listening to the distant hum of the city. Decades earlier, while overseeing a major renovation at the historic Meridian Hotel, a corroded pressure valve had burst, flooding the service tunnels with a thick, acrid cloud of industrial solvents. He had tried to clear the air, but the fumes had seared his lungs and left him coughing violently against a damp brick wall. In the months that followed, what began as a panic attack over a minor plumbing leak solidified into a relentless state of hyperarousal. The smell of paint thinner now hit him without warning, dragging the full, suffocating terror of that tunnel back to him, even though his mind refused to compile the memory into a coherent picture. Those fragmented pieces of the event—just a glare of emergency lights and the metallic taste of fear—would surface randomly, and when those disjointed fragments appeared, the unexplained emotional surge confirmed his growing belief that he could no longer trust his own body. His daily rounds through the hotel’s service corridors became a gauntlet of triggers; when the freight elevator jolted violently on the fourth floor, Thomas’s heart hammered against his ribs and he immediately retreated to the linen closet, convinced the structural supports were failing. His conviction that his body was fundamentally unreliable and that he was entirely helpless to stop bad things from happening directly amplified his sense of immediate peril, cementing his daily reality that he was only truly safe within a two-room perimeter of his apartment. Every unexpected noise in the hallway was treated as a breach of that boundary. As his nervous system remained locked in high alert, the olfactory flashes grew more intrusive, fracturing his remaining composure into isolated shards of panic that refused to connect. When those sudden sensory recollections of burning solvents surfaced, they instantly triggered his nervous system to register danger, ensuring the memory remained a threat rather than a recollection. He knew he could not stop the disaster from repeating itself, so he stopped managing the property floor and instead focused entirely on fortifying his walls. To keep the panic at bay, Thomas turned to sensory overload, cranking the volume on the television or blasting classical music until the walls vibrated, while simultaneously scanning his own mind for any whisper of madness. His unrelenting sense of danger pushed him toward this constant auditory noise, and when the scent of industrial solvent lingered in his memory, the rising dread compelled him to turn up the radio and step further from the window. His constant avoidance of the old renovation site meant he never processed what had actually happened, leaving his fear of sounds and enclosed spaces unchallenged. Each time he reached for the remote or checked the locks, the temporary relief only confirmed his growing conviction that he could never rely on his own mind or body again. Now seventy-six and divorced, Thomas finally scheduled an appointment after a sudden steam vent near his building’s entrance triggered a full physiological collapse, leaving him unable to walk. He sat in the waiting room, his hands clenched around a paper cup of water, terrified that the walls would close in or that his heart would simply stop. What brought him through the door was not a desire to feel better, but a desperate need to understand why his own body continued to wage war against him long after the solvents had vanished. He hoped, more than anything, that someone might finally help him separate the past from the present, before the silence in his apartment became louder than the noise he used to drown it out.
